checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Are deposit requests derived exclusively from block output logs via parse_deposit_requests, not from system transactions?

reachability.notes: If the log parsing is incorrect (wrong contract address, wrong ABI decoding), fraudulent deposit requests could be injected or legitimate deposits could be missed.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate process_general_purpose_requests in fork.py and confirm that deposit requests are obtained solely via parse_deposit_requests(block_output), which reads from block_output logs/receipts. 2. Verify that parse_deposit_requests in requests.py iterates through receipts and filters logs by DEPOSIT_CONTRACT_ADDRESS and DEPOSIT_EVENT_SIGNATURE_HASH. 3. Confirm deposits are NOT derived from system transactions (process_checked_system_transaction is used only for withdrawals and consolidations). 4. Craft a malicious block containing: (a) logs from a non-deposit-contract address with valid deposit event signatures, and (b) logs from the deposit contract with invalid ABI encoding. Verify both are correctly rejected. 5. Verify that extract_deposit_data performs strict offset and size validation for pubkey (48 bytes), withdrawal_credentials (32 bytes), amount (8 bytes), signature (96 bytes), and index (8 bytes). 6. Test with crafted log entries that have correct event signature but malformed data fields (wrong offsets, truncated data, oversized fields) and confirm rejection.

code_locations.line_range: 145-161 (iterates receipts, filters by deposit contract address and event signature)
43-142 (validates ABI encoding offsets and sizes for deposit log data)

Unit test extract_deposit_data with malformed ABI-encoded log data (wrong offsets, truncated fields, oversized fields)
Integration test: submit a block with logs from a contract mimicking the deposit contract address and verify only the canonical deposit contract is accepted
Verify that no code path exists where deposit requests bypass log parsing and are injected via system transaction return_data

The separation between log-based deposits and system-transaction-based withdrawals/consolidations is a critical architectural boundary. Any confusion between these paths could allow deposit injection.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Are withdrawal and consolidation requests processed via process_checked_system_transaction, ensuring system contract failures are caught?

reachability.notes: If the checked variant is replaced with unchecked, system contract failures would be silently ignored, producing incorrect request data. An attacker could manipulate system contract state to cause failures.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. In fork.py, locate process_general_purpose_requests and confirm that withdrawal requests use process_checked_system_transaction (NOT process_unchecked_system_transaction) with WITHDRAWAL_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS. 2. Confirm consolidation requests also use process_checked_system_transaction with CONSOLIDATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS. 3. Verify process_checked_system_transaction raises InvalidBlock if: (a) system contract has no code (len(system_contract_code) == 0), or (b) system_tx_output.error is truthy. 4. Contrast with process_unchecked_system_transaction (used for beacon roots and history storage) which does NOT check for errors - verify this distinction is architecturally correct. 5. Craft a test where the withdrawal request system contract is deployed with code that reverts. Confirm the block is rejected with InvalidBlock. 6. Craft a test where the withdrawal request system contract address has no code. Confirm InvalidBlock is raised. 7. Test that an attacker cannot manipulate system contract state (via preceding transactions in the same block) to cause the checked system transaction to fail or return corrupted data.

Validates code existence and error-free execution, raises InvalidBlock on failure
Contrast: does NOT check code or error, used for beacon roots and history storage

Unit test: call process_checked_system_transaction with a reverting contract, expect InvalidBlock
Integration test: build a block where a preceding user transaction modifies system contract state to cause failure, verify the block is rejected
Differential test: compare block validity outcomes when swapping process_checked vs process_unchecked for withdrawal/consolidation paths

Beacon roots and history storage use unchecked (failure is acceptable), but withdrawal and consolidation MUST use checked.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does validate_header reject blocks with header.number < 1?

reachability.notes: A peer sends a block with number 0. If accepted, it could corrupt chain state or trigger genesis-specific code paths.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate the block number validation in validate_header (fork.py, ~line 357-410). Confirm there is an explicit check: header.number >= 1 (or equivalently, rejection of number == 0). 2. Verify the check is performed early in the validation sequence, before any parent header lookups that might fail differently for block 0. 3. Craft a block with header.number = 0 and submit via P2P. Verify it is rejected with a clear error. 4. Test edge case: header.number = 1 (should be accepted if parent is genesis). 5. Test with very large block numbers (uint64 max) to check for overflow. 6. Verify that genesis block (number 0) is only loadable through the genesis initialization path, never via block validation.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does validate_header enforce strictly increasing timestamps (header.timestamp > parent_header.timestamp)?

reachability.notes: A proposer sets timestamp <= parent timestamp. If accepted, time-dependent operations (e.g., TIMESTAMP opcode, time-locked contracts) could behave incorrectly.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate the timestamp validation in validate_header. Confirm strict inequality: header.timestamp > parent_header.timestamp (not >=). 2. Craft a block with header.timestamp == parent_header.timestamp and verify rejection. 3. Craft a block with header.timestamp < parent_header.timestamp and verify rejection. 4. Craft a block with header.timestamp = parent_header.timestamp + 1 and verify acceptance. 5. Test with timestamp = 0 and parent_timestamp = 0. 6. Test with very large timestamps near uint256 max to check for overflow behavior. 7. Verify that the TIMESTAMP opcode returns the block timestamp, confirming that non-increasing timestamps would affect smart contract execution.

Unit test: validate_header with timestamp < parent_timestamp, expect rejection
Unit test: validate_header with timestamp == parent_timestamp + 1, expect acceptance

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does validate_header enforce sequential block numbers (header.number == parent_header.number + 1)?

reachability.notes: A proposer sends a block with a gap or duplicate number. If accepted, chain continuity is broken.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate the block number sequentiality check in validate_header. Confirm: header.number == parent_header.number + 1. 2. Craft a block with header.number = parent_header.number + 2 (gap) and verify rejection. 3. Craft a block with header.number = parent_header.number (duplicate) and verify rejection. 4. Craft a block with header.number = parent_header.number - 1 (regression) and verify rejection. 5. Test integer overflow: parent_header.number = MAX_UINT256, header.number = 0 (wrap-around). Verify no silent acceptance due to arithmetic overflow. 6. Verify that the check occurs before any state modifications that would be invalid for non-sequential blocks.
executable_checks: Unit test: validate_header with number = parent_number + 2, expect rejection
Unit test: validate_header with number = parent_number, expect rejection
Unit test: validate_header with number = parent_number - 1, expect rejection

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does validate_header enforce parent_hash == keccak256(rlp.encode(parent_header))?

reachability.notes: An attacker creates a block with a parent_hash that does not match the actual parent header hash. If accepted, chain reorganization or fork attacks become possible.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate the parent_hash verification in validate_header. Confirm: header.parent_hash == keccak256(rlp.encode(parent_header)). 2. Verify the parent_header used for comparison is fetched from the canonical chain state, not from user-supplied data. 3. Craft a block with parent_hash set to a random 32-byte value that does not match the actual parent header hash. Verify rejection. 4. Craft a block with parent_hash set to the hash of a different (non-parent) block header. Verify rejection. 5. Craft a block with parent_hash == keccak256(rlp.encode(modified_parent_header)) where the parent has been tampered. Verify the comparison uses the stored (authentic) parent header. 6. Verify that the RLP encoding used for the hash is canonical (no leading zeros, correct list encoding). 7. Test with the genesis block as parent to ensure the hash check works at chain start.

Test integer division edge cases: parent_gas_limit = 1023 (adjustment_delta = 0, meaning gas_limit must equal parent_gas_limit). 8. Test with very large parent_gas_limit to check for overflow in parent_gas_limit + adjustment_delta.
